client: I just got rejected from my top choice university last week, and I can't stop feeling like a complete failure. Everyone around me seems to be moving forward while I'm stuck here questioning if I'm even good enough. I know therapy is supposed to help with stuff like this, but I'm not sure talking about it will change the fact that I wasn't good enough for them.
therapist: I hear how painful this rejection feels, and how it's making you question your worth - that's completely understandable when something we've worked hard for doesn't work out as we'd hoped. I wonder if we could explore together what "being good enough" means to you in this situation?

client: I don't know... I guess being good enough would mean getting that promotion instead of being passed over again. But it's hard to think about that without feeling like maybe I'm just not cut out for this career path. When things like this keep happening, it's hard not to take it personally.
therapist: It sounds like these repeated setbacks are really shaking your confidence in your career path, and that must feel incredibly discouraging. I notice you're connecting these work situations directly to your personal worth - what makes you feel this is about you rather than other possible factors?

client:
I know logically that there are other factors at play - the economy, company budgets, things like that. But it's hard not to take it personally when I keep getting passed over for promotions or my ideas get shot down. It makes me feel like I'm just not good enough no matter how hard I try. 

When you suggest it might not be about me, part of me wants to believe that, but another part thinks "then why does this keep happening to me specifically?" It's like there's this pattern that proves I'm not cut out for this career.
therapist: It's understandable that this pattern feels personal when you're the common thread in these experiences - our brains naturally look for patterns to make sense of things. I wonder if we could explore how you're defining "being cut out for this career" versus what might just be normal career challenges everyone faces?

client: I guess I never really thought about how I'm defining success in my career. It just feels like everyone else is handling the challenges better than me, and that must mean I'm not good enough. But when you put it that way, maybe I am being too hard on myself - though it's hard to believe that when I see my coworkers managing the same pressures without falling apart.
therapist: It sounds like you're starting to notice how comparing yourself to others might be shaping your definition of success, which is an important insight. What would it feel like to consider that your coworkers might have their own struggles that aren't always visible from the outside?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard not to compare when I see my coworkers getting promotions and recognition while I'm stuck in the same position. Even if they have struggles, at least they're succeeding professionally - that's what everyone sees and values. I just feel like I'm falling behind no matter how hard I try.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd feel this way when you're seeing visible signs of others' advancement while your own efforts haven't been recognized in the same way. I wonder if we could explore what "falling behind" means to you personally, beyond what others might see or value?

client:
I guess when I think about "falling behind," it's not just about promotions or achievements. It's this constant fear that I'm wasting my potential and time is running out. But when I try to explain that to friends, they just say "everyone moves at their own pace," which makes me feel even more alone in this. 

The weirdest part is I know logically that comparison is unhealthy, but I can't stop checking LinkedIn and feeling sick when I see former classmates getting ahead. It's like I'm punishing myself on purpose.
therapist: I hear how deeply this fear of wasted potential is affecting you, and how isolating it feels when well-meaning advice doesn't resonate with your experience. What do you think drives you to keep checking LinkedIn even when you know it makes you feel worse?

client: I think I keep checking because part of me hopes I'll finally see something that makes me feel better - like proof that I'm not falling behind. But it always backfires because I end up comparing myself to people who seem to have it all figured out. It's like I'm punishing myself but can't stop.
therapist: It sounds like this checking behavior is almost like an emotional gamble - hoping for reassurance but often getting the opposite outcome. What might it feel like to experiment with limiting these comparison triggers while we work on building your own measures of success?

client: I get what you're saying about it being an emotional gamble, but when I try not to check how others are doing, I just feel more anxious. What if I'm falling behind and don't even know it? The idea of limiting those triggers makes me nervous because then I'm just left with my own doubts.
therapist: I understand how not checking might actually increase your anxiety right now - it's like you're trying to stay informed to manage that fear of falling behind. What if we approached this gradually, perhaps starting by noticing what happens emotionally when you do check, to better understand what need it's serving for you?

client: I get what you're saying, but it’s hard not to check because I feel like I’m missing something important if I don’t. When I do check, I feel a bit of relief at first, but then I just end up scrolling more and more, which makes me even more anxious. I’m not sure if noticing my emotions will really help—it feels like I’ll just get stuck in my head even more.
therapist: It sounds like checking provides a temporary sense of relief, but then pulls you into a cycle that ultimately leaves you feeling worse. I wonder if we could explore together what that initial relief might be telling us about what you're hoping to find or avoid in those moments?

client:
I guess the relief comes from feeling like I'm preventing something bad from happening, like if I don't check the locks five times, my apartment might get broken into. But you're right - after I do it, I just feel exhausted and stupid for wasting so much time on it. 

The hard part is that even though I know logically the chances are low, my brain keeps screaming "but what if this is the one time you don't check?" That fear feels so real in the moment.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming that "what if" feeling can be in the moment, even when you know logically the chances are low. It sounds like checking provides temporary relief from that intense fear, but leaves you feeling drained afterward. What do you think might happen if we experimented with gradually reducing the number of checks while also developing alternative ways to cope with that fear?
